v986: Sanjay's mother died of a sudden heart attack while he was at work. He had spoken to her that morning about something small. In the months after the funeral, Sanjay could not bear Rituparna being out of sight. He called her many times during her hospital shifts and became upset if she did not answer. He asked her to stop visiting her sister on weekends. When she was ten minutes late, he imagined accidents and paced the flat. Rituparna loved him and understood his grief, but she felt suffocated. "I cannot breathe," she told a friend. Sanjay knew he was too much, but his fear felt stronger than his reason. At night he lay awake listening to make sure she was breathing.
v987: This is the loss wound. When someone we love is taken without warning, research suggests the brain's alarm system becomes highly alert to any sign of another loss. Sanjay had also lost a younger brother to fever when he was eight, a grief no one in the family talked about. His mother's death reopened that old wound. Sanjay's style is the outward one, clinging and controlling to stop loss happening again. The inward style would be refusing to get close at all, so loss cannot hurt. Every unanswered call became a trigger that sent his body back to the moment of the phone call about his mother. His heart raced and he could not think clearly until he heard Rituparna's voice.
v988: At a grief group in his church, Sanjay read that "Jesus wept" at his friend's tomb. He realised he had never truly grieved. He began to cry to God about his mother and brother, and his grip on Rituparna slowly loosened.
v989: Set a grief time each day to remember and cry
v990: Agree with Rituparna on one check-in call per shift
v991: Notice the panic and name it as old loss, not new danger
v992: Write a lament for his brother and his mother
v994: The gospel does not ask Sanjay to hide his grief. Jesus "wept" beside Lazarus (John 11:35) and is a "man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief" (Isaiah 53:3). God promises that those who mourn "shall be comforted" (Matthew 5:4) and that "the LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart" (Psalm 34:18). Sanjay's hope is not that Rituparna will never leave, but that God is with him in every loss and that death does not have the last word. As he poured his sorrow into God's care, he no longer needed his wife to carry all his fear. The church group also helped, as other people who had lost parents listened and prayed. His healing came in relationship, not in isolation.
v995: God created us to grieve. Tears, sighs and talking about loss help the body release stress and process what happened. Research suggests that unprocessed grief keeps the nervous system on alert, scanning for the next disaster. When grief is shared with safe people, the brain begins to file the loss as a painful memory rather than an ongoing threat. God also designed marriage to be a safe base, but not a cage. A healthy attachment lets each person go out and come back. As Sanjay learned to trust God's presence, his body could relax when Rituparna was away.
v996: Psalm 34:18|The LORD is nigh unto them that are of a broken heart.
v1000: Within a year Sanjay's calls dropped to one or two a day. Rituparna visits her sister again. On his mother's death anniversary he became anxious and clingy for a week, but he told Rituparna what was happening instead of hiding it. He now speaks about his brother for the first time, and the family has started remembering him together.
v1001: Grief that is shared with God and others loosens the grip of fear.
v1002: Sanjay's mum died suddenly, and he got scared his wife would go too. When he cried to God and talked about it, he felt safer.
v1003: The Fiancee Who Checked His Phone
v1004: Nisha, 27, a nurse, and Daniel, 29, an IT worker, engaged in Ludhiana, Punjab
v1005: Nisha and Daniel were engaged and planning a wedding for December. Daniel was honest and kind, yet Nisha could not stop checking his phone. When he left it on the table, she scrolled his chats. She asked who every female colleague was. If he said he was working late, she messaged his friends to confirm. Daniel had never given her a reason to doubt him, and he was starting to feel like a suspect. "If you cannot trust me now, how will we be married?" he asked. Nisha felt terrible. She knew her fear was out of proportion, but each time she found nothing, the relief lasted only a few hours before the worry came back.
v1006: This is the distrust wound. When Nisha was twelve, she discovered that her father had a second family in another city. For years he had lied about business trips. Her mother pretended nothing was wrong. Nisha learned that people who say they love you may be hiding something and that you must find out before you are fooled. Her style is the outward one, investigating and controlling. The inward style would be refusing to commit or keeping a distance so no one can betray her. Research suggests that checking brings brief relief, which teaches the brain to check again, like a loop. Her body reacts to a locked phone screen as though it is her father's lies all over again.
v1007: In premarital counselling, Nisha read that "perfect love casteth out fear." She realised she was trying to make Daniel perfect so she could feel safe. She began to bring her fear to God, who never lies.
v1008: Agree on a no-checking rule with an honest open-door policy
v1009: When the urge comes, wait twenty minutes and pray
v1010: Tell Daniel the fear instead of investigating
v1011: Explore her father's betrayal with a counsellor
v1013: The gospel heals distrust by showing a God who is utterly faithful. "God is not a man, that he should lie" (Numbers 23:19). Jesus calls himself the truth and says "the truth shall make you free" (John 8:32). Nisha's father broke trust, but her heavenly Father keeps every promise. That does not make all people safe, but it gives her a secure base from which to take wise risks. Love "believeth all things, hopeth all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7), not naively, but with eyes open. Nisha also confessed her checking to Daniel and asked for forgiveness. Daniel chose openness instead of resentment. Together they are building trust through honesty, repair and prayer, which is how the relational gospel works.
v1014: God designed trust to be built through repeated experience. Research suggests that each time a person keeps a promise, our brain updates its prediction and feels a little safer. Checking interrupts that learning, because the brain credits the checking, not the person, for the safety. When Nisha resists checking and sees Daniel stay faithful, her nervous system can learn a new truth. God also made us to need honest relationships, and confession brings what is hidden into the light. As Nisha practises trust with God and Daniel, her alarm system can begin to quieten.
v1015: Numbers 23:19|God is not a man, that he should lie.
v1019: Nisha has not checked Daniel's phone in three months, though she still feels the urge on hard days. Twice she gave in and confessed it the same evening. Daniel shares his plans more openly, and they pray together before bed. The wedding is going ahead, and Nisha is continuing counselling about her father.
v1020: Trust grows when we stop checking and start telling the truth about our fear.
v1021: Nisha kept checking her fiance's phone because her dad had lied. She learned God never lies, so she can tell Daniel when she is scared.
v1022: Filling the Emptiness With a Screen
v1023: Karthik, 33, a sales manager, and Divya, 31, married with a toddler in Bengaluru
v1024: Karthik scrolled his phone for hours every night. He watched reels, played games and chatted with a former classmate who praised his posts. Divya felt invisible. When she tried to talk, he nodded without looking up. One night she saw a message from the classmate saying, "You deserve someone who appreciates you." Divya was crushed. Karthik insisted nothing physical had happened, and that was true, but he admitted he had been looking forward to those messages more than to coming home. Underneath, he felt empty and like a failure. His sales targets were slipping, and he felt he was not a good enough father. The phone gave him a quick feeling of being noticed.
v1025: This is the inadequacy wound. Karthik's older brother was the family star, a doctor praised at every gathering. Karthik was always compared and found lacking. His parents said, "Why can't you be like your brother?" He learned that he was not enough and that attention had to be earned. His style is the outward one, chasing attention and filling the emptiness with screens and outside admiration. The inward style would be giving up on trying and hiding from challenges. Research suggests that likes and messages trigger small bursts of dopamine that briefly lift mood, but they cannot satisfy the deeper need to be valued. The more he scrolled, the emptier he felt, and the more he scrolled.
v1026: When Divya confronted him, Karthik broke down. In prayer he heard the words "complete in him" from Colossians 2:10. He realised he had been hungry for a love that no screen could give, and he asked God and Divya for forgiveness.
v1027: End all private chats with the former classmate
v1028: Put the phone in another room after nine
v1029: Confess honestly and give Divya a full apology
v1030: Spend twenty minutes each night talking with Divya
v1031: Meet a trusted man from church weekly for accountability
v1032: The gospel tells Karthik he is already enough in Christ. "Ye are complete in him" (Colossians 2:10). Jesus said, "I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger" (John 6:35). The emptiness Karthik felt was real, but it was a hunger for God's love and his family's closeness, not for a stranger's praise. God "satisfieth the longing soul" (Psalm 107:9). Healing also required confession and repair. "Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed" (James 5:16). Karthik's apology to Divya was the start of rebuilding trust. A brother from church walked with him weekly, so he was not fighting alone. Grace did not excuse what happened, but it gave him the courage to face it.
v1033: God created us with a reward system that helps us seek good things like food, connection and meaningful work. Research suggests that phones and social media can hijack that system with quick, easy rewards. Over time the brain wants more and enjoys less. But God also designed us to find deep satisfaction in real relationships and in his presence. Eye contact, touch and honest conversation release calming chemicals that build lasting bonds. As Karthik turns toward Divya and God, his brain slowly relearns where true satisfaction is found.
v1034: Colossians 2:10|And ye are complete in him.
v1038: Rebuilding trust took months. Divya had days of anger and doubt, and Karthik had nights when he relapsed into scrolling. But he no longer hides it. They now take a walk together after their son sleeps. Karthik says he still feels inadequate at times, but he brings that feeling to God instead of to his phone.
v1039: Only God's love and real closeness can fill the emptiness we try to fill with screens.
v1040: Karthik felt not good enough, so he looked for praise on his phone. He learned God already loves him, and he put the phone down to talk with his wife.
v1042: Manoj, 40, a contractor, and Sunita, 37, a homemaker, married fifteen years in Patna, Bihar
v1043: Manoj had a quick temper. When dinner was late or the children were noisy, he shouted, slammed doors and once threw a plate against the wall. He had never hit Sunita, but she was afraid of him. When he exploded, she went completely silent, staring at the floor, unable to speak. Later she felt numb for days. Their children tiptoed around the house. After the plate incident, their twelve-year-old daughter hid under the bed and would not come out. That shook Manoj. He went to his pastor and said, "I am becoming my father. I need help." Sunita spoke separately with a woman counsellor from the church about her own fear and safety.
v1044: This is the violation wound, on both sides. Manoj grew up with a father who beat his mother and him. He learned that power and loudness keep you from being hurt. His style is the outward one, becoming the aggressor. Sunita's father also had rages, and she learned to freeze and disappear. Her style is the inward one, going silent and shutting down. Research suggests that when the brain senses threat, it can fight, flee or freeze. Manoj's nervous system jumps into fight, and Sunita's drops into freeze, which is why she cannot speak. Both are old survival responses, but they keep each other trapped. Anger is never an excuse for frightening others, and Manoj is responsible for his behaviour.
v1045: Manoj read Ephesians 6:4, "provoke not your children to wrath," and realised God's fatherhood was nothing like his father's. Sunita learned that God is "a refuge for the oppressed," and that safety mattered to him.
v1046: Make a safety plan for Sunita and the children, including a safe place and trusted contacts
v1047: Manoj agrees to leave the room before shouting and to join an anger programme
v1048: Both meet separately with trained counsellors before any joint sessions
v1049: Sunita practises grounding to come out of freeze
v1050: Rebuild trust slowly through consistent calm behaviour
v1051: The gospel never asks anyone to stay in danger. God is "a refuge for the oppressed, a refuge in times of trouble" (Psalm 9:9), and he cares about Sunita's safety. If anyone is being hurt or threatened, getting to safety comes first, and the church should help. For Manoj, the gospel offers both truth and grace. He must own his anger fully. "Cease from anger, and forsake wrath" (Psalm 37:8). Yet he is not beyond hope. Christ took our sin so that Manoj can be made new, a different kind of father. Healing came through confession, accountability with a mentor and counselling. Sunita is learning that her voice matters to God, who "healeth the broken in heart" (Psalm 147:3). Any reconciliation must follow real, proven change.
